IoT Hydroponic Grow Bed

Final-year project — low-cost Deep Water Culture system for small-scale spinach farmers in Kitwe, Zambia

ESP32 pH sensor BH1750 light sensor Peristaltic pump Blynk IoT

An ESP32 reads pH and light levels continuously, triggers a peristaltic pump to dose nutrients, and switches a relay-controlled grow light — all monitored remotely through Blynk. A mobile dashboard shows live light and pH readings over Wi‑Fi. The build targets farmers who can't afford commercial hydroponic controllers.

±0.5 pHsensor accuracy after calibration

Testing showed the light sensor and relay to be reliable. The pH probe was the hardest part: it needed repeated two-point calibration against pH 4.0 and pH 7.0 buffers before readings stayed stable. Dosing was slower than planned because of the long tubing.

States of Consciousness

Written at Livingston Research · about 800 words

EssayPsychology

The states of consciousness are associated with the level of awareness of a person. When in a state of daydreaming, a person may exhibit low awareness and once they are brought back to reality by an external or internal factor, they might display a high level of awareness. Furthermore, people who experience sleep paralysis are said to be in a state of consciousness, yet they cannot move. This, in turn, results in high level of awareness and a feeling of suffocation as well as fear. In addition to that, a person may be in a state of consciousness where they are asleep, yet they can still hear what is happening around them. However, even in a state of deep sleep, some external factors such as an alarm ringing in real life can become part of a dream, but you never really realize where the sound is coming from until you wake up and see your alarm ringing.

Read the full essay

When I contemplate upon the mind of a human in association with states of consciousness, I am reminded of a smartphone. In the event that it is not touched or disturbed for a period of time, the illuminance of the screen reduces, before it crosses over into what is referred to as sleep mode. In humans, “sleep mode” happens in situations where a person becomes detached from the current moment while awake — this is known as a daydream.

At one point or the other in the past 24 hours, I did not even realize that I was daydreaming until the plastic chair I sat on shook me back to reality when it suddenly tipped back a bit in a failed attempt to make me fall down. At that moment, I became more aware of the people all around me and in view of that, my palms became sweatier than usual despite the cold weather as I listened to the sound of my own heartbeat. Then it followed that a voice from behind me whispered, “Your chair is broken”. An elderly woman pointed to a vacant seat in front of me, yet despite how aware I was of each detail around me, I could not process the fact that there was an empty seat in front of me and I could have easily stood from the broken chair and sat there instead.

That incident haunted me so much that I could not even remember the walk back home. I was not even aware of how tired I was until I fell on the bed and drifted off to a sleep, of which I was aware of all the prominent sounds around. My eyes were closed, yet I felt annoyed by the sound of paper being crumpled and the voices that accompanied it. At one point or the other I must have fallen into deep sleep, or so I assumed.

In my dream, there was a sound of which I did not know the source. I looked around to no avail until I slowly woke up and realized that my alarm was actually ringing in real life, but the sound somehow managed to penetrate my dream.

Kendra Cherry (2020) a cognitive psychologist, accounted for the fact that a person’s state of consciousness is linked to their level of awareness. On one hand, a person who is in a state of drowsiness experiences low awareness while on the other hand, when a person is exposed to a stimulant, they have a heightened level of awareness.

A time I recall being extremely aware of my surrounding is when I faced sleep paralysis for the first time. I was conscious, yet I could not more and this alarmed me more than I already was. The more I tried to fight it, the more I felt suffocated, as if all the air was being drawn out of my lungs. When I finally woke up, I turned back to the memory and could not decide if indeed I was conscious, or it was some kind of lucid dream, all I am sure of is all my fears came crashing down on me at that point in time.

Last but not the least, during lectures, I am in a state where I am present in the room, but my mind is somewhere else. I hear what the lecturer is saying, but my brain cannot always retain the information. This is often accompanied by exhaustion that disappears immediately when the lecture is done.

Lastly, it is worth noting that many times the state of consciousness goes hand in hand with the awareness of a person. Low awareness is due to states such as daydreaming or drowsiness, while high awareness comes about from being in a state of consciousness like sleep paralysis, which can be frightening.

References

  • Kendra Cherry (2020). State of consciousness, understanding human consciousness. www.verywellmind.com/lesson-four-states-of-consciousness-2795293

Children and the Media

Written at Livingston Research · about 1,500 words

EssayMedia & child development

The media can either provide an environment from which a child can flourish as they develop self-awareness and identity or, it could negatively affect them to the point where they have low self-esteem and self-hatred. Nevertheless, other aspects such as family, friends, exposure to new culture and school can influence a child, but the media is most predominant source of influence because 21st century children are exposed to new technologies every day. Everywhere you go, you see a child playing games on their phone, singing along to the latest pop hits, talking about the newest movies and trying to learn the trending TikTok dance. All this may be a lot of fun, but it may have a lot of harmful effects on children that range from eating disorders because they want to have “the perfect body” for a trend to fear because they see people constantly dying from corona virus. Luckily, there are measures that can be taken to ensure that a child is benefiting from the media more positively than negatively.

Read the full essay

Under scrutiny, it is not difficult to make out the fact that children, at one point or the other, become imitators of the people with whom they associate and the television shows they set their curious eyes on — this is their unique way of learning more about the surrounding environment. However, this new exposure to the media can prove to be influential to children in both the safe and harmful sense. Discussed below are some of the factors that influences children, what the media is and how it affects children, as well as what can be done to increase the positive outcomes of it and decrease the undesirable effects.

What influences children

Researchers have established that a number of environmental and social aspects influence children at distinct periods of their development. Take for instance the prenatal period where the fetus responds to the voice of its mother and develops a fondness towards it. In this case, the mother has the most power over the child until the period of toddlerhood when the toddler develops a sense of autonomy and their interest in other children increases.

Moreover, when children reach the middle childhood period, they explore more and more of the world beyond the walls of their home, make friends who have a behavior and mind of their own and receive invitations to festivals that expose them to new culture which open them to different ways of life other than the one they have known since birth.

Additionally, public schools are said to impact children more than home-schools. Educational psychologists, in lieu of the American Psychological Association, published their views on home-schooling in the APA Monitor (Murray, 1996). The psychologists warned parents that their children may experience difficulty joining “mainstream life” and may not grow up to be “complete people” if taught at home. A study revealed that parents of those whose children attended public schools reported that 61% believed homeschooled children were isolated (Gray, 1993). One participant described the majority of homeschooled children as “socially handicapped”.

The Media

The word media emanates from the word medium, which means ‘Go between’. Thus, the media refers to technical devices that make possible the dissemination of information all across the world to various people. This information can either be in electronic or print form which encompasses; newspapers, television, social media, music, and movies.

Whether the media impacts children positively or negatively depend on how much care is taken by parents and adults in monitoring the shows aired on television screens, the music played on radios on the drive to school, the content on their devices and even the pictures depicted around the house. All these little details have power over the mind of a child as they develop self-awareness and identity.

Take, for example, the famous cartoon Cinderella about a woman mistreated by her stepmother and stepsisters. In as much as it attempts to teach the importance of kindness, parents must also take into consideration the fact that children may misunderstand and instead interpret the film in the sense that all stepmothers and stepsister are evil.

How the Media Affects Children

According to an article published on an Australian parenting website, television, YouTube, games and movies affect children of different ages in different ways.

Although babies are attracted to bright light, movement, and activity on TVs, phones and computers, their ability to comprehend the situation shown is very limited as their brains cannot understand simple plots. Often time, they can only differentiate real life from the fictional TV world when they are about 18 months old.

Additionally, babies might familiarize themselves with characters after a period of time and may even copy simple actions such as clapping from TV shows, but are more likely to do it with their parents and siblings. However, babies begin to apply what they see on a screen to real life situations when they are about 2½ years old.

For preschoolers of 0-8 years, a fearsome picture or anecdote is all it takes to upset and alarm them as these depictions can remain vivid in their mind for days even months. Despite the warning displayed on television right before a graphic scene, preschoolers might choose to ignore this and copy the violent behavior because children tend to follow the visual part as opposed to the non-visual parts such as speech.

Furthermore, when children advance to year five, they start taking keen interest in contemporary music. If they view sexualized images, videos, and dance moves, they might copy them because their favorite artists are doing it.

School-age children have the ability to follow simple plots and recognize how these events are connected to each other. Despite this, children take things as they are and will not stop to critically analyze what they see on TV and social media platforms such as TikTok that have a very unpredictable "for you" page. One moment a child may be watching an educational video on numbers and the next they may be watching a video that encourages bullying.

What is more, role models such as TV characters and social media celebrities may influence the personality, behavior, and attitudes of school children since they idolize those people on will listen to and imitate every single thing they do; be it a silly trend or simply the vocabulary they use.

Unlike preschoolers, school-age children depend less on visual image, yet the statements and images they see and read on new platforms may scare and anger them because they are aware of the fact events such as death and crime are real.

Studies have shown that media violence has more of an adverse effect on school-age children than younger children. This is because, video games and Television shows communicate that violence is okay when the hero uses it for a virtuous cause. Therefore, children may misunderstand this and think that violence is the way to solve conflict and acquire what you want when you want it.

To finish, sexualized pictures and videos can alter how boys and girls think, see and feel about themselves and their bodies. All of a sudden, it is repulsive to have acne, and you are considered unattractive if you do not have a body as curvy as Kim Kardashian or are not as tall as your Marvel Idol Chris Hemsworth. This can reinforce self-hate and a negative body image in children as they approach adolescence.

Conclusion: What could be done to increase positive media.

The media — television, music, movies and social media — is known to be toxic and addictive. Nevertheless, measure can be taken to boost positive media and protect children from the dark side of the media.

We oath to read reviews on the internet or even make an effort to watch children movies before it is shown to them. If the film is seen to be unsuitable for the young audience it was made for, a film can be rated with zero or one star and a review left to communicate to other people how truly inappropriate the film is.

In addition, entertainment providers have come with what is known as parental lock. This can be used to block channels that are unfit for children of certain age groups. This, therefore, ensures protection of children from any form of graphic material.

Providing children with books, music, movies, and games that promote self-love and harness positive body image helps children to realize their worth and prevents them from falling into situations such as self-harm, isolation, depression and eating disorders.

Lastly, keeping a close eye on children and the celebrities they idolize could be of great help when it comes to protecting a child from developing bad language, unruly behavior and negative self-image. If anything, we should protect both ourselves and children from the negative effects of the media.

References

  • Wartella, E.A., & Lauricella, A.R. (2012). Should babies be watching television and DVDs? Children, Adolescents, and the Media, 59(3), 613-621. doi: 10.1016/j.pcl.2012.03.027.
  • Zimmerman, F., Christakis, D., & Meltzoff, A. (2007). Television and DVD/video viewing in children younger than 2 years. Archives of Pediatric and Adolescent Medicine, 161(5), 473-479. doi: 10.1001/archpedi.161.5.473.
  • Gray, S. (1993). Why some parents choose to home school. Home School Researcher, 9(4), 1-12.
  • Gabriela Martorell. Child 2e
